nuggets.text: Use the `@for` loop in Angular v17 syntax to iterate over the collection.
Apply the `ngClass` directive to an actual HTML element within the `@for` loop.
If using a `div` element, place the `ngClass` directive on the `div` within the `@for` loop.
If avoiding the `div` element, apply the `ngClass` directive to the `span` element instead.

original.scored_text:
Your edit identifies the key point: `*ngFor` repeats the element carrying the directive **and its children**, not just its children. Page 1 explains that Angular expands the shorthand into an `<ng-template>` containing the original element.

For your original example, the repeated content is therefore the entire `<div>`, including its `[ngClass]` binding and `<span>`. Preserving that structure means keeping the `<div>` and its binding within the repeated content, rather than leaving one `<div>` outside it.

The provided reference does not cover Angular v17’s `@for` syntax, so it cannot establish the official migration syntax.

# Use *ngFor to list objects in component

This tutorial lesson demonstrates how to use `ngFor` directive in Angular templates in order to display dynamically repeated data in a template.

<docs-video src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/eM3zi_n7lNs?si=MIl5NcRxvcLjYt5f&start=477"/>

## What you'll learn

* You will have added a data set to the app
* Your app will display a list of elements from the new data set using `ngFor`

## Conceptual preview of ngFor

In Angular, `ngFor` is a specific type of [directive](guide/directives) used to dynamically repeat data in a template. In plain JavaScript you would use a for loop - ngFor provides similar functionality for Angular templates.

You can utilize `ngFor` to iterate over arrays and even asynchronous values. In this lesson, you'll add a new array of data to iterate over.

For a more in depth explanation, please refer to the [Built-in directives](guide/directives#ngFor) guide.
